## Appendix A: Matrix Geometry, Restrictions, and Sandwich Constructions {.unnumbered #app-ch9-a}

This appendix derives the results that Sections 3.2 and 5.1 used. It is
reference material: the exercises do not require it, and the main route is
complete without it. Complete R reproductions of every construction below
belong to the Computer Lab tasks on normal equations, on manual HC3, and
on the joint Wald helper.

### Projection and the normal equations {.unnumbered}

Let $\mathbf X$ be $n\times p$ with full column rank, so $\mathbf X'\mathbf X$
is invertible. The least-squares criterion is
$S(\boldsymbol\beta)=(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)'(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)$.
Expanding gives
$S=\mathbf y'\mathbf y-2\boldsymbol\beta'\mathbf X'\mathbf y
+\boldsymbol\beta'\mathbf X'\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$, and differentiating
with respect to $\boldsymbol\beta$ yields the normal equations

$$
\mathbf X'\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\mathbf X'\mathbf y,
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
\mathbf X'(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})=\mathbf 0 .
$$

The second form is the geometry: the residual vector is orthogonal to
every column of $\mathbf X$. Hence
$\widehat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\mathbf H\mathbf y$
with $\mathbf H=\mathbf X(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'$, and
$\mathbf H$ is symmetric and idempotent — the orthogonal projection onto
the column space of $\mathbf X$. Its trace is $p$, which is why the
leverages $h_{ii}$ sum to the number of fitted coefficients; for `m2` they
sum to 6.

Two consequences used earlier follow immediately. Any full-rank recoding
$\mathbf X\mathbf A$, with $\mathbf A$ invertible, spans the same column
space, so $\mathbf H$ and $\widehat{\mathbf y}$ are unchanged: releveling
a factor or centering a predictor cannot alter a single fitted value.
Adding a genuinely new column enlarges the space and can change every
fitted value. And under the classical error model,
$\widehat{\mathbf V}=s^2(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}$ with
$s^2=RSS/(n-p)$, which is where every classical standard error in this
chapter came from. Section 3.2's check confirmed both the coefficients and
the orthogonality to about $10^{-13}$ on the occupation model.

### General linear restrictions {.unnumbered}

Let $\mathbf R$ be $q\times p$ of rank $q$ and consider
$\mathbf R\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf r$. Since
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ has covariance
$\sigma^2(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}$ under the classical model, the vector
$\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r$ has covariance
$\sigma^2\mathbf R(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf R'$. Standardizing by
that covariance and dividing by $q$ gives

$$
F=\frac{(\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r)'\,
[\mathbf R(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf R']^{-1}\,
(\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r)}{q\,s^{2}},
$$

which has an exact $F_{q,\,n-p}$ reference under normal errors, because
the numerator and denominator quadratic forms are independent chi-squares.
This is the same number the extra-sum-of-squares formula produces: fitting
the restricted model and differencing residual sums of squares is an
algebraically equivalent route. Taking the two rows of $\mathbf R$ that
select `typeprof` and `typewc`, with $\mathbf r=\mathbf 0$, returned
0.0319 in Section 3.2 — the adjusted type block test, obtained without
fitting the reduced model.

The equivalence with the extra-sum-of-squares route is worth seeing once.
Minimizing $S(\boldsymbol\beta)$ subject to
$\mathbf R\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf r$ with a Lagrange multiplier gives the
restricted estimator
$\widetilde{\boldsymbol\beta}=\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
-(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf R'
[\mathbf R(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf R']^{-1}
(\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r)$, a correction applied
only in the directions the restriction touches. Substituting it into the
criterion shows that the increase in residual sum of squares is
$RSS_R-RSS_F=(\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r)'
[\mathbf R(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf R']^{-1}
(\mathbf R\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\mathbf r)$, which is exactly the
numerator above. Fitting the reduced model and differencing, or evaluating
the quadratic form in the unrestricted fit, are two routes to one number.

Replacing $s^2(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}$ by a robust covariance in the
middle of this expression gives the Wald statistic of Section 5.2. The
algebra survives the substitution; the exact reference distribution does
not.

### The HC3 sandwich {.unnumbered}

Write the coefficient error as
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\boldsymbol\beta
=(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X'\boldsymbol\varepsilon$. Under
independent rows with possibly different variances $\sigma_i^2$, its exact
covariance is

$$
(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}
\Big(\sum_i\sigma_i^2\,\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i'\Big)
(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1},
$$

a *sandwich* with the design component as bread and the error-scale
component as filling. The classical estimator substitutes a common $s^2$,
which collapses the filling to $s^2\mathbf X'\mathbf X$. The HC family
substitutes each row's own squared residual instead. Because
$E(e_i^2)=\sigma_i^2(1-h_{ii})$ under the classical model, the raw
residual understates the error at high-leverage rows; HC3 corrects by
dividing by $(1-h_{ii})^2$, which is deliberately slightly conservative
and performs well in small samples [@mackinnon1985; @long2000].

Building the estimator directly — inverting $\mathbf X'\mathbf X$ for the
bread and forming the cross-product of the rows of $\mathbf X$ scaled by
$e_i/(1-h_{ii})$ for the filling — reproduces
`sandwich::vcovHC(m2, type = "HC3")` to within about $10^{-12}$ on the
occupation model, which is floating-point agreement.

### The CR1 cluster sandwich {.unnumbered}

Cluster robustness changes the filling, not the bread. Partition the rows
into $G$ clusters and let $\mathbf X_g$ and $\mathbf e_g$ hold cluster
$g$'s rows and residuals. The cluster score
$\mathbf s_g=\mathbf X_g'\mathbf e_g$ sums the within-cluster
contributions *before* the outer product is taken, so the estimator
retains the within-cluster residual correlations that the independent-row
filling discards:

$$
\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{CR1}}=c_G(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1}
\Big(\sum_{g=1}^{G}\mathbf s_g\mathbf s_g'\Big)(\mathbf X'\mathbf X)^{-1},
\qquad c_G=\frac{G}{G-1}\,\frac{n-1}{n-p}.
$$

If every cluster held one row, the filling would reduce to the HC0 form,
which is why a row-level robust SE is the special case that assumes away
the dependence. The asymptotics are in $G$, not in $n$: 3,745 pupils in 79
schools supply 79 independent pieces of information for this covariance,
which is why the clustered SE of 1.8476 is so much larger than the
row-level 1.0377 and why a $t_{G-1}$ reference is used. Constructing the
score matrix by summing $\mathbf X\odot\mathbf e$ within school, applying
$c_G=1.0131$, and sandwiching it reproduces
`sandwich::vcovCL(..., type = "HC1", cadjust = TRUE)` to within about
$10^{-13}$ on the observed-reading STAR model.

## Appendix B: Bootstrap Schemes and Intervals {.unnumbered #app-ch9-b}

Section 6 used case resampling and said why. This appendix runs the other
two schemes on the same model, the same three targets, and the same seed,
and defines the two higher-order intervals named there. The lab tasks on
resampling variants and on manual covariance reproduction carry the full
implementations.

### Residual and wild resampling {.unnumbered}

Both schemes hold the design matrix fixed and rebuild outcomes from the
fitted values. Residual resampling draws leverage-rescaled residuals
$e_i/\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}$ with replacement and adds them to the fitted values,
which assumes the rescaled residuals are exchangeable across rows. The
wild bootstrap keeps each row's own rescaled residual and multiplies it by
an independent mean-zero, unit-variance draw — here $\pm1$ with equal
probability — so each row retains its own error scale.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{26\baselineskip}
```

```{r}
#| label: ch9b-schemes
#| echo: true
set.seed(90909)
X <- model.matrix(m2); e <- residuals(m2); h <- hatvalues(m2)
fit_draw <- function(y) {
  b <- coef(lm(y ~ X - 1))
  c(b["Xeducation"], b["Xtypeprof"] - b["Xtypewc"], b["Xtypeprof"])
}
residual_draws <- t(replicate(B, fit_draw(fitted(m2) +
  sample(e / sqrt(1 - h), replace = TRUE))))
wild_draws <- t(replicate(B, fit_draw(fitted(m2) +
  e / sqrt(1 - h) * sample(c(-1, 1), nrow(d), replace = TRUE))))
rbind(case = apply(draws, 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE),
  residual = apply(residual_draws, 2, sd), wild = apply(wild_draws, 2, sd))
```

For the education slope the three schemes give 0.3699 (case), 0.2820
(residual), and 0.3673 (wild). The residual scheme is the outlier, and its
value sits close to the classical 0.2752 — which is what one should
expect, since both assume one common error distribution. The wild
bootstrap, which does not, lands near the case result and near HC3's
0.3823. For the professional coefficient the pattern repeats more
strongly: 1.9926, 1.4861, and 1.9767. When the schemes disagree, the
disagreement is about the error model, not about the data, and it is a
reason to say which scheme was used.

### Percentile, normal, and higher-order intervals {.unnumbered}

Four interval definitions are worth distinguishing in words.

- The **percentile interval** takes the 2.5th and 97.5th quantiles of the
  resampling distribution of the estimate.
- The **normal-approximation interval** takes the original estimate plus
  and minus 1.96 bootstrap standard errors. It uses the resampling
  distribution only for its spread, so it is insensitive to skewness.
- The **bootstrap-$t$ interval** resamples a studentized quantity,
  $(\widehat\theta^{*}-\widehat\theta)/SE^{*}$, and inverts its empirical
  quantiles. It needs a standard error inside every resample, which is
  expensive, and it is more accurate when the studentized quantity is
  closer to pivotal than the estimate itself.
- The **BCa interval** adjusts the percentile endpoints for median bias
  and for an acceleration constant that captures how the standard error
  changes with the parameter. It is the usual recommendation when the
  resampling distribution is visibly skewed [@efron1993; @davison1997].

For the three targets of Section 6 the skewness values $-0.3891$, 0.2635,
and 0.3785 are mild, so percentile and normal-approximation endpoints agree
closely and the higher-order corrections would change little. That
agreement is a property of this example, not a general licence.

### Extended practice: resampling choices (Integrative) {.unnumbered}

1. Repeat the case bootstrap of Section 6.2 for the women coefficient in
   `m2`, with the same seed and $B$. Report the bootstrap SE and
   percentile interval, compare them with the classical 0.0097 and the
   HC3 0.0079, and explain what it means that the classical SE is the
   largest of the three here. State what the comparison does not show.
2. Resample the STAR observed-reading records in two ways: drawing pupils
   with replacement within each school, and drawing whole schools with
   replacement. Report the resulting SEs for the small-minus-regular
   difference beside the row-level 1.0377 and the clustered 1.8476.
   Explain which resampling unit the design supports and why, and say
   what neither scheme repairs.
